utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before beginning, good morning. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the registry staff, the counsel for the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence, and good morning to General Krstic. Before we actually begin, I would like to say that today we are going to work in the morning until a quarter past 12.00, and after which we will have a break of an hour and a quarter, which means we will resume at 1.30 to go on until 4.30. I don't know if everyone has been prepared for this. We ourselves were rather surprised. Because we have to free the courtroom for that period. So I would like to know from the parties whether this will cause any inconvenience. The Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problems so far as we are concerned as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Another question has to do with the ruling of last Monday. The Chamber confirms its oral decision regarding the motion to decide whether the statements, intercepted statements of the accused came under the provisions of Rule 66(A) or 66(B). The Chamber maintains its oral decision and ruling that those statements fall within the category of Article 66(B); in other words, they are not preliminary statements in the sense of Rule 66(A) but are documents in the meaning of Rule 66(B). As for the other party [as interpreted] regarding the late use of these radio intercepts by the Prosecutor, the Chamber will be rendering a written decision, and I think that things will be much clearer in that way, and they already are clearer. That is, the Chamber will be rendering a written ruling regarding that motion. So we are now in a position to begin. Witness, could you stand, please. Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Please make yourself as comfortable as possible. Thank you very much for coming. First you will be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. I think it will be in the person of Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could go into closed session very briefly for his background. I've discussed this with Defence counsel and there was no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, Mr. McCloskey, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, as this witness has a pseudonym, we need to establish the link between his name and the pseudonym. So perhaps you could write down the name of the witness, the name and the pseudonym, and obtain from the witness confirmation before we continue, as we're still at the level of identification of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You should have a yellow sheet with his name from yesterday, but here's a new sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you see your name written on this piece of paper? Is that indeed your name? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness FF, before joining the Interception Unit of the Bosnian Muslim army, did you have an interest in and a hobby in ham radio operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. As a 10-year-old boy, I joined a radio club in Banovici in those days, and I learnt about electronics, Morse's code, and all the other things linked to ham operations, and I'm still an active member of ham association. Developing my work as a radio amateur, I passed all the tests so that I received the highest possible qualification in that field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Interception Unit for 2nd Corps, where were you assigned in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: In July 1995, we were on Mount Konjuh, where we had been ever since June 1993, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position on Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I was platoon leader, consisting of two squads in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I later acquired a rank, that is, in 1994, the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard quite a bit about the various procedures in your work there, so I will not go into that with you, but what I do want to ask you about is various notebook entries, printout entries, and in one case, an actual audiotaped conversation. So I first want to direct your attention to Exhibit 747, which is to your left, but if you could look at the original notebook. First of all, if you could find Exhibit 747. Its a photocopy to your left. And if you could actually go to the original notebook, which is on your right, and if you could go to the area marked there where there are two conversations, and if you could just take a look at those two conversations. What pages are they on the original notebook? I'm referring to the conversations one at 1240 hours and one at 1300 hours. I would just like you to confirm, if you could, that the photocopies in Exhibit 747 are the identical and exact copies of the material in the original notebook which is next to you regarding especially those two conversations I referred to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, for me to find it in the copy. Is it this conversation at 1350 hours?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1240 and 1300, in your handwriting, on the day where the little yellow marker is, the ones we've discussed in my office, noted between Krstic and Popovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Then it's not what has been marked in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It should be in the other notebook. I'm sorry. You're exactly right. And it's the second --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: In the other one, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, here it is. 1240 and 1300 hours. Those are the times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's Exhibit 835. Sorry, it's Exhibit 844.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, that's it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Looking in Exhibit 844, is that an exact copy of the two conversations that I mentioned earlier, 1300 hours and 1240 hours, from the original notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They are true copies of my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you the person that listened to the conversation and transcribed it in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that done at the time noted in the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, the same day. After the conversation was recorded, it was taken down in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now if we could do the same thing for one other conversation, and that is in the original notebook I had you looking at, which is Exhibit 747. And the conversation I would like you to confirm is in Exhibit 862/A at 10 hours, between a Mandzuka and a General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it in the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you could find it in the copy of the original notebook, which is 747.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That is a conversation at 10.00 between Mandzuka and General Krstic, and is that particular conversation in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No, this is not my handwriting. This is the handwriting of another operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the notebook at 747 is an accurate and a true example of the kinds of notebooks that were used by you and your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I can confirm it because I know the kind of notebooks we were given to write in, and also I have had two notebooks here in front of me, and the two are identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you determine from the notebook the conversation between Mandzuka and General Krstic, what date it occurred on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: This conversation, the date of the conversation can be determined on the basis of the computer-typed text. Here in the notebook it would take a little longer to find it, because the date was not indicated every day. But if you were to take all the notebooks into consideration, then one could establish the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you go to Exhibit 860/A and B, which should be that printout that should be right to your left, and 860/B is the actual Bosnian version of that. Could you take a look at the conversation noted at 10.00 between Krstic and Mandzuka? Does this appear to be the kind of printout that would have been sent to headquarters after such a conversation was transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. That is how we worked. It was printed out with a header, with the information regarding frequency, the participants in the conversation. So that is how we worked, so that could be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also looking at Exhibit 862/B, which is just a photocopy of the original notebook of this particular Mandzuka/Krstic conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. That is the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again referring to the printout, what time, according to the printout of this Mandzuka/Krstic conversation, or what date was this conversation of 10.00 a.m. actually intercepted on, based on the printout? And again, that's Exhibit 860/B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The conversation is on the last two pages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, and the date the 2nd of August, 1995 is clearly indicated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the conversations between Krstic and Popovic, one first at 1240 hours and then the next at 1300 hours. And first of all, looking at the notebook, can you determine the dates of those two conversations that you actually took down from the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, because the date the 2nd of August is indicated after the transcripts of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you work your way back to determining your conversations are actually on the same date, August 2nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: It can be seen by the time when it was noted in the notebook, the first one at 1240 and then the next one at 1300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now if you could go to, I believe, Exhibit 852/A and B, which is a printout, and 851/A and B. 851/A and B and 852/A and B should reflect the printouts of these two conversations. And if you have a chance to look at 852/A and 851/A, do those represent printouts of those two conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What dates are reflected on those printouts for the two conversations between Krstic and Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: On the printouts the date is the 2nd of August, 1995, the same date as in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's for both conversations, at 1300 hours and at 1240?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibits 850/A and 853/A are photocopies of the notebook entries, and I'll just have the witness confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just for clarification, since there's so many intercepts floating around here, I know that the two which have the conversations between General Krstic and Popovic, I know they're history. But these other three, or these other ones that we're now talking about, have they been introduced in evidence previously or is this the first time they're coming in? Just so I get my -- everything straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am talking right now about three intercepts, two that he actually took notes on and one that he recognised someone else taking notes on, all occurring on August 2nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand the two, or at least the two I -- the Krstic/Popovic ones. Okay. I'm clear. I'm not clear about the other ones, whether they're already in evidence or being introduced for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. Like the two I've just mentioned, this is also a new conversation. It is a Krstic/Mandzuka conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. Thank you. I mean, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was provided at the same time to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So if you could just take a quick look at 850/A and B - it would be 850/B for you, and 853/B - to confirm that those are accurate photocopies of the material in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: 853/A is. I'm looking at it now. And 851/B; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me now. That too is an original copy of the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I believe the witness has said all we need him to say on these three conversations, and I would, to try to clarify these conversations, I would just read them into the record. That would be my request, or Your Honours may just purely read the conversations if you would like, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The first conversation at 1000 a.m. is between Mandzuka and General Krstic, 862A. M: Hello, General. It's all OK. I'll be done today. I'm up here at Sokolina and Bandijera. It looks as though they're planning something. K: Uh-huh. And how did it go? M: We just have a few down in the creek. Some of them have gone through, about 1,000, of them. K: You shouldn't have let any of them escape. M: We didn't dare to cross over into the other state. We just checked the terrain by helicopter yesterday. It's pretty inaccessible. Did you see how the Serbian Ministers accepted them over there like liberators? Even the Red Cross came. K: Where were they met? M: In Bajina Basta. K: Register all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: K: Register all R.S. /Republika Srpska/ Muslims over there so we can use them for exchange. How many more are down there? M: About 2.000 altogether. Beara went over there to Serbia. He'll take care of it. There are some captured and dead. Those who crossed the river threw away their weapons while those who headed for Kladanj were probably armed. K: They threw away their weapons over there. There are some down there towards Srebrenica. Search everything. M: Everything is going according to plan, General. K: Good. Good bye. The next conversation, Exhibit 850A, at 1240 hours between Krstic and Popovic: P: It's Popovic. K: Krstic. P: Go ahead, boss? K: Get on over to Bajina Basta, you and Kosoric. You know what you have to do. P: Yes. K: Is that clear? P: Clear. K: If necessary, give me a call from somewhere. Have we understood each other? P: Understood. Has he set out from up there towards me? K: Who? P: Pero, in fact, Cica. K: He is on his way, fuck him. P: He went up there because we had some parcels, to check what they know. K: Good. P: He is up there at Trnosavac. K: Good. Get in touch with him and straight on to Bajina Basta, as soon as possible. P: Clear. K: Go on. P: Bye. The next conversation at 1300 hours, OTP Exhibit 853A, between Krstic and Popovic: K: Yes? P: Hey, boss. K: Go ahead. P: Beara has just called me. He came back from there this morning. K: Yes. P: He said he reported to Miletic. K: Yes. P: There are about 500 - 600 of them over there. K: Did you understand me, man? What do we have to do with them up there? P: It's like this. They don't allow anyone to talk with them at all. K: Is that clear to you, Popovic? P: Yes. K: You and KOSORIC go straight on to Bajina Basta. Do you know what you're supposed to do? P: He tells me: You'll go there for nothing. K: Get in touch with that MARKOVIC, the commander of ... battalion. P: Yes. K: I want you to bringing me Turks back here. Is that clear, man? P: Well, everything is clear to me, except if they won't give them? K: What do you mean, they won't give them? P: Well, they won't give them. K: They're our Turks, man! P: Well, the MUP /Ministry of the Interior/ doesn't allow any access. K: What? P: The MUP doesn't allow access, do you understand? K: I'll turn the gun-barrels on them. Did you understand? P: Understood. K: That's it. Go there as soon as possible. P: Understood. K: Go on. P: Good. K: Bye. P: Bye. Now, Your Honours, I will now ask the witness -- there is one more exhibit in this case which I'll ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you had a chance to hear a taped account of the conversation between Krstic and Popovic that took place, according to these memos, at 1300 hours on August 2nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if what you heard on the tape -- I see Mr. Petrusic standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to object. I consider that the witness should, first of all, have to say whether he taped the conversation and whether he transcribed it and then whether he heard the tape, listened to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I believe when we went through the notebook on this 1300 hours conversation -- did you have anything to do with this transcribing of this conversation at 1300 hours, on August 2nd between Krstic and Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. I recorded the conversation and transcribed it from the tape to the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the normal course of your duties and the normal process that you and the rest of your people did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then the tape that was played in my office, do you know -- was that tape related to the conversation in the notebook of the 1300 hours conversation, August 2nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. What I heard was that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, at this time, I would offer to play the actual original tape. We have a tape, Exhibit 854, for evidence, but with our problem yesterday, I think we should be ready to play again the original tape of this conversation. And if I could ask the interpretation booth not to translate for this, if we could just listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we start up again? The transcript of this is Exhibit 854A. I've got it, but I'm not sure that everyone else has had a chance to look at it. If they could get it in front of them, that would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That would be a good idea, to have the transcript before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have the English on the ELMO. If everyone has it and you've, I'm sorry, managed to get the tape back to where it should be started, then we can play it again. I apologise to the booth for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness FF, is that the conversation that you heard on August 2nd and transcribed in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic for the cross-examination. Please go ahead. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of your work at the intercept centre where you worked, did you have occasion to hear the voice of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how you could arrive at the conclusion, the undisputed conclusion -- can you explain how you could arrive at the conclusion, the undisputed conclusion, that in a particular case it was, in fact, General Krstic's voice if he failed to introduce himself on the radio device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krstic usually did give his name. Not only did we know his voice, we knew many of the voices of the other officers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular conversation, Exhibit 854, which has just been dealt with by the Prosecutor, we have none of this identification, that is to say, General Krstic does not identify himself. Were there any characteristic traits of voice on the basis of which you were therefore able to arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, not only me. We all knew General Krstic by his voice because he was present for a long time on the frequencies, in conversations. So we were able to do that and we always knew. We were able to confirm not only him, but we knew many of the officers by listening to their voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that he was on the air for a long time, the conversations that you tapped into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the period which my testimony relates to. He was the Commander of the Drina Corps and before him there was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to be more concrete and give us a time. What time period? And please wait for me to finish my question and make pauses between question and answer, please. You say the Commander of the Drina Corps. What period was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I can't give you precise data. I didn't think it necessary to remember them, and a lot of time has passed since then, so I can't give you an exact date, but from the documents and how he moved around in the service, that is something that is a known factor. And Krstic was not unknown to me from previous periods at the other battlefield, Olovo battlefield. I know that he lost a leg there in the operations there. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to this particular period. You say that it was the period when he became commander of the Drina Corps and that before him it was Zivanovic. I'm not interested in a date. I'm not interested in a date when he became commander of the Drina Corps. What I'm interested in is the time frame that you intercepted him, monitored him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I know that it was before the operations at Srebrenica that he was there, he was present there, so we know him since before, since before the events that I am testifying to now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific, because it's not very specific.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. I don't remember the event exactly. I didn't attach importance to it. I did not know that I would be called upon to testify, to remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness FF, I'm not linking you to this event and the conversation of the 2nd of August. All I'm asking you for is the time frame when you monitored this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I don't want to say something that I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or any of your colleagues from the intercept centre have occasion to -- that is to say, before you began doing work of this kind, interception and monitoring, did you in any way -- did you have an undisputed sample of General Krstic's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at one point able to have a definite sample of General Krstic's voice, either by radio, television, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No. Before the war I never even knew or heard of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: During the war -- well, you're asking me before, a certain sample before I began doing my work. No, I did not. Only during the period when I was actively engaged in that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness FF, did you record a conversation between General Krstic and a certain Mandzuka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No. I said I did not, that it was not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you did not introduce it into the notebook? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No, I did not introduce it into the notebook, because it's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this notebook, which bears the number 748 [sic], or rather notebook 103, is there a conversation there which you intercepted and allegedly registered the voice of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Mandzuka conversation, now you're asking me something that I'm not quite sure what you're asking, because this conversation with Mandzuka is not my handwriting, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to help counsel, that notebook 103 is 747, for the record, not 748.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I misspoke. Thank you very much to my learned colleague for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, that conversation was not recorded by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have looked through the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. I have the conversation with Mandzuka in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the preparations and testimony, you have had a chance to look through the notebook, have you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look through the entire notebook; I just looked at this particular conversation. I didn't leaf through the notebook further, because the Prosecutor just asked me to state my views on this particular conversation in the notebook, so that I didn't go through the rest of the notebook. I didn't leaf through it. I don't know what you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you, as you did not record that conversation, whether in that notebook 103, or Exhibit 747, whether there is any conversation there of General Krstic which you took down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. On the next page there is the conversation between General Krstic and Cerovic, for example. Here I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness FF, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I noted down that you had the highest possible qualifications in ham operations and Morse code. What were these operations? Could you give me an idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of my work as a radio ham, a radio amateur, I still maintain communications according to international regulations with the International Radio Ham Union, and I have links with radio hams throughout the world, all over the world, at certain frequencies and with certain types of operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it is strictly technical, but you have no -- you didn't have any background in recognising voices, studying phonetics, being able to detect voices from their timber and their -- would it -- was that also included in your studies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No, it was not included. But quite simply, when you do a particular kind of work for a long time, just as you know your friends by their voices, you can recognise the voice of people you have heard very often, regardless of whether we have had special training with that or not, at least as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it possible in the intercepts -- were the intercepts clear enough for you to affirm that that would be the voice of someone, usually? Could you detect them with certainty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because they were conversations most often which -- the other type of conversation, like you and I are having now, that kind of thing, clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it as clear as that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it was fairly clear, yes, because they are open conversations. They were not encrypted, protected in any way, or passed through any devices which would distort the voices in any way. They were our natural voices and they were fairly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in the intercepts where General Krstic did not introduce himself or announce himself, was it referred after that to experts to know who it was, or it was you directly who decided who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, not directly me. Every operator, once he had recorded a conversation, he would decide whether and who was doing the talking, on the basis of a voice or the self-identification. That's what he would do. And then he would write it in if he was certain who was the party to the conversation. And if not, then very frequently we could identify individuals by saying 1, 2, 3, depending on how many participants. If we were not sure of who was taking part in the conversation, we would put 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you had a double qualification, to intercept and to decide who it was, if he was not announcing himself? It was all in your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, but we didn't have any orders to that respect that we had to identify the speakers. We just did it sort of along the way, without -- well, quite simply, we would recognise or not recognise a voice, and that's what we would do. Nobody asked us or demanded that we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, you can affirm that even though General Krstic did not announce himself, this was his voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, and not only me; we all knew that, all of us working there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You would compare sometimes your intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't remember comparing them, because quite simply, the message was recorded and then it was transcribed into the notebook from the tape, from the notebook into the computer, and thus it was dispatched to the headquarters and command, or wherever we sent it on, and we didn't go back to those conversations again. We would continue monitoring, recording, intercepting, and the same procedure would be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, I have just one question. In Exhibit 854/A, which is a transcript of the conversation between Popovic and Krstic, allegedly, at the top of it it says: "Transcript of conversation taken from the tape between users O (Operator); O1 (2nd Operator); X (Popovic's boss); and P (Popovic)." Is there any reason why, if Krstic's voice was immediately identifiable, the top of it says "Popovic's boss" rather than identifying who he was? The transcript that's sent on, or the communique that's sent on, which is 852/A, to the higher command identifies it as participant Krstic, Popovic, but I was just wondering why that identification isn't made in 854/A. There may be a reason I don't understand. I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In the conversation in 854/B, there was an introduction. Popovic says, "I need Krle." That is how he called him, either using the word "boss" or "Krle." So we can see from that that it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that reasoning. I just didn't understand why the heading didn't identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The transcript is an OTP product that we did of the original tape. I should have made that clear. That is something that our office did. That is not a product of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it's a translation, authentic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We have done a very careful transcript in Serbo-Croatian and a translation of that transcript, but that is a product of our Translation Unit and our transcribers of that tape. The other -- all the other products are Bosnian government products, but the transcriptions of tapes are OTP products. We did not get any taped transcriptions, that I'm aware of, from the Bosnian government, just tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And so 854/B, which is the Bosnian, B/C/S, is subject to the same explanation? Because that too just has "Operator" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Mr. President. These are OTP products of the Translation Unit and our team transcriber, and they developed these headings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Witness FF, I have three questions for you. The first: Do you remember the first time that you heard the voice of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but it was much earlier than these documents were written, the ones I am testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have any idea -- even though you can't remember when was the first time, do you have any idea of how you came to the conclusion that it was General Krstic's voice when you heard it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I've told you already that in addition to General Krstic, we recognised many other officers by their voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I'm referring to the first time. The first time you heard my voice you didn't know it was my voice. So the first time, if you have any idea, how was it you concluded that it was General Krstic's voice? Did someone tell you that was General Krstic? Did the voice say, "I'm General Krstic"? Or was there some other means whereby you were able to conclude that that was General Krstic's voice and from that moment on into the future you knew it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, yes. Mr. Krstic tended to introduce himself, as he did in the conversation of the 2nd of August. Later on you hear in this conversation Krstic. He identified himself. So that is what he did earlier on too. So I think it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But imagine if you didn't hear the conversation from the beginning when the person introduced himself; you intercept the conversation halfway through. Would you be in a position to know that it was General Krstic's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any such conversation here, but in many cases it was possible to conclude - not just with respect to him, but others - even if we didn't start recording from the beginning, it was possible to know who was talking, in many cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question, Witness: For how long did you listen to the voice of Krstic in all? Mr. Petrusic asked you for the dates, end dates, the beginning and the last time. I'm asking you for the period of time during which you listened to General Krstic's voice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I heard him certainly several tens of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several dozens of times? Over a period of how long? Eight months, one year, two years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Roughly throughout the year 1995, almost. I can't say the whole of it, but most of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having listened to the voice of General Krstic throughout this period, were there any particular characteristics of his voice which allowed you to identify it? You already knew the voice, but was there any some particular characteristic of his voice that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I never really studied the timbre of people's voices or any such thing in particular, but I recognised it more or less. I recognised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Witness FF. Thank you for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. However, I think that Mr. McCloskey has something to tell us, so with respect to the documents used during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have Exhibit 854, which was the tape and the transcript, Exhibits 853, 850, 851, 852, 860, 862, and 844, which is a notebook under seal. That reflects all the various notebooks and printouts that I was referring to. And for the Court's background, and this will be dealt with in a little bit more detail, the notebooks and the printouts were received in our office in December, and we have been analysing and transcribing and translating those since December of last year, 2000, and the actual tape that we just heard was received in a consent search of October, and we've identified -- October of 2000. We identified that tape in November of 2000. The tape of the Krstic/Popovic conversation and the notebook and materials were sent to the Defence on January 17th of this year, shortly after we had fully analysed them. The full notebook, 103, was sent on January 26th of this year, and we will provide you with the actual declarations and some of the chain of custody evidence in the following witnesses, but that's just to give you the background into that as it, I believe, is relevant to the motion that is before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something? Just what you just said, just so I understand it, you're saying that the two Popovic conversations which you sought to introduce, and the third conversation which the General Mandzuka, that you did not have them in your possession at the time that General Krstic was being cross-examined; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. It was October, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: October 31st or November 1st was the time of his ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We received the notebooks in December, and we got them back to the office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you say, "We received them," I just want to -- does that mean that that was the first time it came to the attention of the Prosecution? I'm not saying this has happened, but they're lingering in a pile someplace and somebody finally got their eyes on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've done that over the years. However, this particular set was actually picked up from the 2nd Corps in a mission that was in December 2000, and, I believe, was back in our office on December 15, 2000, and then we have been working on those ever since. It was a lot of material. The tape that we just heard came in a bit earlier. The consent search was October -- around October 19th, and we've identified it as the conversation in November. We've noted this in the motion. I believe it was the -- we were able to pin it down to, I think, the first or second week in November, and once we heard on it the tape, then we -- and then we picked up this other material and we eventually found it in the material, the notebooks and the printouts, and we then, soon thereafter, sent it off to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That tape was before the cross-examination on 31st October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Another team had picked it up on the 19th, and we were able to review their material in November. On November -- either the first or second week of November, we found -- we found this particular tape. So it wasn't in our possession very long, and it was in another team's possession. We found out that they had searched Muslim archives, so we were interested, and we were able, through a log that you will soon see, identify this particular conversation. Then we started looking at it very soon after that. This will be dealt with in a bit more detail with the actual witnesses that were involved in this chain of custody, but it will come in, as you know, slowly, and, in some cases, it gets a little confusing, but hopefully this will give you a good road map to the next evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But just to pin down this, at the time that you were cross-examining General Krstic, you didn't have this tape? You didn't know about this tape? You hadn't identified the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we did not know about it. It was in -- I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Someplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis may clear me up on this, but it was in OTP possession in another team, in our evidence locker, shortly after the consent search which was between 11 and 19 October 2000. So actually, during the cross-examination, this tape was sitting with, probably with 30, 40 others in a locker. Eventually, we were able to find the Bosnian log that went to all those tapes, and by reviewing the log, though they misspelled General Krstic's name, we were able to find it in early November, after the cross-examination of General Krstic, as far as I know, but the cross-examination and Judges' questions went on for a while, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, regarding the admission of documents and also would you respond to these allegations, if I may call them that, of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence maintains its general objection regarding the documents that we made yesterday, but taking into consideration all that has been said by Mr. McCloskey, it is our submission that the admission of these documents, and especially the tape he refers to, because there's mention of the month of October, that it was in the OTP but in the hands of another team, and of course when they got hold of it after the cross-examination, we feel that this type of evidence could more appropriately be introduced in the reopening of the case by the Prosecution than in the rebuttal case of the Prosecution. That is our position. But in any event, we'll wait for the ruling of the Trial Chamber in writing, which will resolve many dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. McCloskey on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't imagine you want to hear oral argument on the motion, so I won't get into that, though I will try to clarify also the three SDB tapes that Mr. Harmon referred to yesterday came in at the same time as the other notebook material I spoke of and was turned over in, I believe, the same time frame to the Defence, and I -- the motion, I won't get into the details, but Defence counsel never specifically dealt with the details of why they felt that these Krstic/Popovic conversations should fall under the same argument as the other "kill-them-all" conversations specifically. I think they made a general argument. We made a same general argument and did not deal with them specifically, and I won't get into any arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you wish to respond now to this additional opinion that you just heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Witness, please don't move for the moment. We need to pull down the blinds for you to be able to leave safely. Thank you very much once again for coming. I will ask the usher to pull down the blinds and to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're now going to have a 20-minute break. I should like to inform the parties that in the afternoon, Judge Fouad Riad will not be present because he has some medical examination, so we will sit in incomplete composition, without Judge Riad. So a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for that tardiness. I think that we have Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have the next witness here, and Your Honour, we'd like to have his testimony heard in closed session. I understand our colleagues in the Defence have no objection to this, and if the Court would like to hear the reasons for the closed session, I'm very happy to provide them in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of March, 2001, at 9.20 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at, 4.45 p.m.,
